Kallas, a former Estonian prime minister and one of the EU’s most vehement Kremlin critics, is also seen by many as an unlikely interlocutor for Putin. Moscow has placed her on a wanted list, while Russian officials have made clear they have little appetite for engaging with her.
Reinier van Lanschot, a Dutch member of the European parliament, has called on EU leaders to convene a summit and agree on a single representative to engage with Putin.
He said: “The EU must speak with one voice, and Ukraine must always be involved. If you take those two things into account, then I think it makes perfect sense for Europe to engage in talks.”
But he acknowledged that reaching a unanimous agreement would be difficult, with any proposed appointment potentially vulnerable to a veto by a single member state.
In the meantime, this week’s Nordic initiative could encourage more European politicians to establish their own channels to Moscow, said Linnainmäki.
“It’s inevitable that politicians around Europe will now raise the question: if the Finns and Norwegians are calling Putin, why should our country not do it?” he said.
Beyond the question of who should speak to Putin lies a more basic question: whether there is any point in Europe talking to him at all.
Raik warned that Putin might interpret Europe’s sudden interest in reopening dialogue as a sign that Ukraine and its allies were growing desperate, with Kyiv facing a difficult winter.

“My concern is that the way the Kremlin is reading this step now is that the Europeans are in trouble, the Ukrainians are in trouble,” she said. “Knowing how Putin looks at Europe, I think he’s always keen to try to use opportunities to create divisions, or at least appearances of division,.”
The Kremlin’s account of Tuesday’s conversation offered little indication of any change in Putin’s maximalist demands for ending the war.

According to the Financial Times, Putin spent part of the conversation lecturing the Nordic leaders on medieval Slavic history, repeating pseudo-historical arguments that have long been used to question Ukraine’s right to exist as an independent state.
Still, Moscow has appeared more willing to entertain European involvement in diplomacy since US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg last week.
Moshes suggested that Moscow was tiring of Trump’s unpredictability and looking to Europe as an alternative, calculating that the US midterms could leave the president politically weakened.
But Putin’s willingness to take the call should not be mistaken for a readiness to compromise, Moshes cautioned.
“It doesn’t mean we are moving anywhere towards a ceasefire, let alone peace, because it’s clear that Putin’s plan A is a military defeat of Ukraine.”
Shaun Walker contributed reporting

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s defeat is a major blow to Trump and his orange wave
articles.summary: The far-right candidate was supposed to claim the presidency, but Brazilian voters had other ideas
body: For Donald Trump, Brazil’s presidential election was meant to represent the crest of the “orange wave” – a three-year surge of rightwing triumphs that has reshaped Latin American politics in the US president’s tangerine-hued image.

The far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, was supposed to claim the presidency on Sunday, bringing the region’s biggest democracy and economy into Trump’s orbit, after similar victories in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Honduras, Ecuador and Peru – not to mention the capture of Venezuela’s government after the country was invaded in January.

But Brazilian voters had other ideas, turning out in huge numbers to vote against the pro-Trump populist and return the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to power. On Tuesday, as Lula celebrated his 81st birthday to the sound of samba in Brasília, Bolsonaro fled to Miami on a private jet.
“This is a significant blow, indisputably, to Trump’s regional strategy,” Benjamin Gedan, the director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, said of Bolsonaro’s defeat.

“[Trump] was perceived to be steamrolling over South America, having invaded Venezuela and seen close allies win elections in Argentina and Chile, in Bolivia and Colombia. That momentum had given the impression that he could determine political outcomes throughout Latin America – and he clearly enjoyed it,” added Gedan, a former White House South America adviser.
“This is a region where he was really perceived to have a successful foreign policy, and this just flies in the face of that image.”

The US setback was celebrated in China, whose rapidly growing influence in Latin America Trump has been trying to combat with his so-called “Donroe doctrine” of regional domination. “[Lula has] effectively thwarted Trump’s strategy for the region … Trump failed to bring Brazil, the largest nation in South America, under his sway,” Hu Xijin, a prominent Beijing propagandist, enthused on X.
Trump has responded to his ally’s failure by halfheartedly querying the election, which Lula won by 4.3m votes.

“I think the election was really strange … It’s so terrible to see,” he told reporters. “But I wasn’t involved,” Trump added, despite a months-long campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure apparently designed to boost Bolsonaro.

Despite Trump’s decision to offer shelter to Bolsonaro – who is facing several criminal investigations in Brazil – many observers suspect the US president is unlikely to pick a major fight with Lula over his rightwing ally’s plight.

“One of Trump’s good qualities - and I mean this sincerely, even though it sounds ironic – is that he can smell a loser, and he wants to be around winners,” said Michael Paarlberg, a former Latin America adviser to Bernie Sanders.
Related: Lula supporters celebrate shock election victory – in pictures

Paarlberg noted how Trump got along with leftist “winners” including Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum; New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – and even Lula himself. “I like Lula, I get along with him very well,” Trump said this week.
“He will certainly favour his ideological co-partisans,” Paarlberg said of Trump, “but if the stink of loserdom starts to waft over them, he will drop them.”

The “stink of loserdom” certainly wafted over Bolsonaro as he fled into Argentina on Tuesday and caught a private jet to Florida, where he briefly declared himself Brazil’s “true president-elect” before apparently changing his mind.
Brazilian social networks filled with memes mocking the far-right politician who, only hours earlier, had vowed to stay in Brazil to lead opposition to Lula.

One particularly scathing internet joke featured a photo of Bolsonaro and a parody of his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan, which was “God, Homeland, and Family.” “Goodbye, Homeland and Family,” it said.
Speaking at his birthday party, Lula said: “This is what the Bolsonaro family is like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US.”

Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, claimed Bolsonaro’s movement – which was founded by his jailed father, former president Jair Bolsonaro – was dead in the water after Sunday’s defeat, although the losing candidate secured 59.8m votes.
“I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Amorim said, recalling how the movement had lost two successive elections to Lula, in 2022 and 2026.
Amorim predicted a more reasonable conservative movement would replace Bolsonaro’s “extremist” one and called his loss “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.
Under Lula, Amorim indicated Brazil would not join Trump’s controversial Shield of the Americas “counter-cartel coalition” – as Bolsonaro had planned to do.

But Amorim also signalled that Lula would pursue pragmatic ties with Washington. “[Trump] has a certain level of pragmatism. They know Brazil isn’t just any old country. So I think we’ll seek to have proper, balanced relations without failing to defend our interests, but without being needlessly hostile, as we’ve always tried to do,” he said, recalling Lula’s good rapport with George W Bush.
Amorim attributed Trump’s questioning of Brazil’s election to “incorrect things” that “rightwing radicals from the state department” had put on his desk.

On Monday, Trump’s former chief strategist, Steve Bannon, urged Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to sever diplomatic and trade relations and “shut down everything with Brazil” as a result of the election supposedly being “stolen up in your face”.
Paarlberg said Trump’s remarks – criticizing the election, but emphasising his fondness for Lula – suggested he would not take Bannon’s advice.

“I read that as: ‘I will give you [Bolsonaro] moral support, but nothing else,’” Paarlberg said. “He certainly wasn’t saying: ‘I’m going to call for further tariffs, or further visa sanctions or any further actual measures to try to punish the Lula government.’”
Gedan was unsure about Trump’s next move. “Anything’s possible, and I’m certain he has no idea how he’s going to approach it either,” he said.

But Gedan believed Trump and Lula could patch things up – perhaps striking a deal involving Brazil’s massive critical mineral reserves – despite Trump’s hopes of a “glorious return” for the Bolsonaros being dashed.

“There’s actually quite a bit of space for a positive relationship, if Trump does not decide to explode US-Brazil relations,” he said. “I think you absolutely could see Trump finding a way to admire Lula’s political skills.”

articles.title: Hello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcry
articles.summary: Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’
body: The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.

Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.
In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.
Related: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey

The backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit of Japan’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.
Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.

The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.
In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.

Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.
“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”
The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.

Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off a diplomatic row in November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.
Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.
China is a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.
The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.

The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé was dropped by several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred to Mao Zedong as a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Everything you need to know about Burnham’s first budget
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: There’s help on household energy bills and a modest bank tax, but big questions about this government’s long term vision remain unanswered
body: Good morning. As chancellor John Healey delivered the first budget of the Burnham government yesterday afternoon, the now-familiar phrasings were all in there: “breathing space” for households, “growth in every postcode,” and setting the foundations for a “radical rewiring of the state.”
But political ambition met economic reality, as the chancellor hammered home the scale of damage inflicted on the public finances by the war in the Middle East.

Just over 100 days into Andy Burnham’s premiership, this was not the all-guns-blazing transformative change of a government that styled itself as the most radical since Margaret Thatcher, but a confetti of micro-measures in a budget so quiet it at times barely whispered. Which is just what the City ordered, rewarding Burnham and Healey with a day of falling bond yields. But was this really the first step in kicking 40 years of neoliberalism into touch?

This morning I’ll take you through the key takeaways, and address the one question nobody else dares to: if this budget was a New Order track, would it be more Regret than True Faith? But first, the headlines.

Spain | Spain has begun three days of mourning after a high-speed rail collision – its second this year – killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
US midterms | Barack Obama, speaking at a campaign rally in suburban Atlanta, offered a closing argument for Democrats in the final week of the midterm election campaign.
UK news | Tommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison after being found guilty of harassing two journalists to the point it caused them fear of violence.

Israel | Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu had lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.

Media | Two news organisations have a duty to the public and their sources to publish allegations of exploitative sexual behaviour by a well-known figure despite claims he is “highly likely” to attempt suicide, the high court has heard.

Compare John Healey’s comms with the pre-budget media blitz of previous chancellor Rachel Reeves (which resulted in a gripping row about productivity forecasts, requiring everyone to pretend they understood what fiscal headroom was). The run-up to this year’s budget was – to the entertaining chagrin of some Westminster commentators – leak-free, with the precision-controlled release of ‘everyday fixes’, such as removing tariffs from 100 food items, from baked beans to boiled sweets – a move promptly dismissed as gherkinomics by the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith.

But was this controlled media strategy simply because there wasn’t… that much to leak? To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, Healey leaned into incremental change, rather than radical transformation, as he warned the Commons that the country was facing not light fiscal headwinds but “global economic storms”.

Indeed, after Healey finished speaking, the government’s independent forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, issued a sharp downgrade to its growth forecast for 2027, warning British households face a “pretty grim picture” for living standards as Trump’s open-ended war on Iran triggers a fresh cost of living crisis. He nonetheless promised a series of fixes to help with the cost of living, including the one measure that could plausibly be described as the proverbial hat-exiting rabbit, a new £100 energy payment for millions of households. But more difficult decisions were delayed until next year’s spending review.

In his 56-minute speech, Healey’s major announcements included plans to: * Give 20m households in council tax bands A to D in England a £100 household energy payment this winter, with equivalent funding for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (immediately after the announcement, Andrew Sparrow over on our politics live blog discovered that gov.uk’s council tax band checker had glitched under the strain.)
* Extend the VAT cut on electricity until July 2027, which Healey says will take £50 off the annual price cap.

* Abolish standing charges, a fixed daily fee on top of usage, on gas bills – this should save two-thirds of us an average of £45 a year, and is likely to help poorer households, which use less gas, so the standing charge makes up a bigger proportion of their bill.
* Extend the 5p fuel duty cut to July 2027.
* Introduce a new Pension Tax Allowance for lower income pensioners that means they won’t be taxed on any of their state pension.
* Abolish the controversial cliff-edge rule for carers’ allowance, a scandal exposed by the Guardian last year that has plunged hundreds of thousands of unpaid carers into life-changing debt.
* Ditch plans to slash the annual cash Isa allowance, overturning the decision by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to cut the amount you can save in tax-free accounts from £20,000 to £12,000 a year.
* Help for the high street: small business rate relief raised from £12,000 to £18,000

* Extra economic and military support for Ukraine worth £10bn based on loans and export finance guarantees, Healey said President Zelensky had told him “you’ve made my day” when he shared the details ahead of the budget speech.

Sticking with Labour’s pledge not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance, Healey raised the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for the next 15 months. He said this would pay for immediate support with energy bills, but campaigners and organisations like the TUC, which has been pushing for a much higher surcharge, will probably be disappointed he didn’t go further for longer. He said the support package would also be paid for by an unexpected two percentage-point income tax rise for landlords and non-Isa savers.

Healey also raised taxes on higher stakes gambling machines by 5% to 25%, and excluded adult games centres as well as vape shops from business rates relief. Other measures include a clampdown on online sellers like Amazon, eBay and Temu avoiding VAT on their platforms, and stronger compliance powers for HMRC to collect overdue tax.

* The National Minimum Wage is to rise by 3.9%, but Healey faces fierce criticism for not fulfilling the manifesto pledge to equalise the lower minimum wage paid to people under 21 with the rate for older workers.

* Healey rejected calls by senior Labour MPs to raise capital gains tax to the same levels as income tax after influential figures, including the former Treasury minister Jim O’Neill, warned it would harm incentives for “wealth creators”.
* The chancellor was reported to be considering lowering the threshold for Reeves’s mansion tax from £2m to £1.5m, but London MPs pushed back.

* Although government departments are facing real-term cuts, Healey made no mention of topping up their cash budgets. Paul Johnson, former director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, suggested the real story of the budget was Labour kicking the can down the road.
“We know who we are, we know where we’re going, we can see the Britain we want to be,” Healey concluded with a flourish, before sitting down for a big hug with Andy.

But did his budget bring British voters any closer to knowing what the Burnham government stands for? Responding to Healey’s speech, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said that most people listening would think “is that it?” And this question was being posed by critical friends of Labour too.

The chancellor was careful to acknowledge the staging posts to come – substantial reports from Alan Milburn and Stephen Timms, on Neets and Pip respectively, will be published next month and offer more detail on proposed changes to welfare spending. The spending review next spring will set out plans to meet Nato commitments on defence. But in the interim, did Healey offer enough? As Andrew Sparrow pointed out, perhaps sensitive to the charge that there is not much radicalism to see here, both Healey and Burnham are presenting the changes to gas standing charges as the start of an ambitious reform of “our broken energy market” – while accepting that “won’t happen overnight”. Government ministers talking up the budget in the evening media rounds also pointed to the section of the budget detailing Healey’s “roadmap for fiscal devolution” as further evidence of the vision thing.

Our early analysis suggests he is at least speaking people’s language. The £100 energy payment targets the struggling middle as well as poorer households, help for local high streets will be popular – while he successfully avoided measures that might anger vocal vested interests (looking at you, Farmer Hoggett). The public is unlikely to shed a tear for gambling bosses or banks. “Nonetheless it comes with risks,” says our political correspondent Peter Walker, “particularly if the smattering of cost of living measures are not properly noticed by voters.”

Meanwhile, our Opinion panel offers mixed reactions. Rohan Sathyamoorthy points out the “outrageous” absence of real help for young people, nor any mention of the student loan crisis. While Polly Toynbee suggests we hold our nerve, and hope, the chancellor did well to choose popular targets and tell the truth about the state we’re in.

And yet again, there’s that awkward question about boldness, and where it’s got to. As my First Edition colleague Hettie puts it so well in the panel: “Small, short-term fixes and making it easier to cancel your Netflix subscription don’t equate to a political philosophy, let alone a programme capable of convincing voters that difficult trade-offs – whether on defence spending or the costs of an ageing society – will be worth it.”
I had to double take when looking at this week’s My Best Shot: the story behind Holly Lynton’s picture of a bare-handed beekeeper. Rather him than me … Michael

At a time when the biggest headlines in football centre on corruption and fraud, Barney Ronay’s column perfectly summarised why Harry Kane winning the Ballon d’Or made so many football fans feel genuine joy. Dipo Faloyin, newsletters team
The New York Times has a fascinating report (£) on a secret plan, hatched up by Alaska Democrats, to pull support from a Republican candidate with sneakiest of tactics. Michael
There is much to admire in Kate Hutchinson’s fascinating and wide-ranging interview with Peven Everett, who has spent the past two years battling stage four cancer. Dipo Faloyin, newsletters team
I really appreciated Dahlia Scheindlin’s early analysis of the Israeli election results, even if the outcome itself is utterly depressing. Michael
Football | Liverpool won penalty shootout in which there were five failed kicks 6-5 after a 1-1 draw with Chelsea in the Carabao Cup at Anfield.

Prem Rugby | Prem Rugby and the Rugby Football Union have stated they are committed to expanding the top flight with English clubs in response to a report claiming that two Welsh sides could soon join the competition.
Cricket | Carey and Inglis counterpunch to put Australia on top in South Africa, to reach 330 for four at the close.
“£100 handout – but Healey warns of ‘global storms’”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The budget dominates the papers, with the Telegraph writing “Healey puts squeeze on savers”, the Express has “Really, is that it, Mr Healey?”, the FT splashes “Healey hits savers in modest Budget”, while the Mirror’s take is “For the many not the few”. The i Paper goes with “Chancellor hands £100 to millions for energy bills – but delays welfare reform and cuts”, the Times says “Healey offers cold comfort” and the Mail’s headline is “This had all the cha-cha-cha of siesta hour in a Mexican border town. Hombre Healey is a snoozer!”. Metro leads on “A £100 trick or treat?” and the Sun rates what won in the budget with “Shirkin’ workin’ gherkin”.
Burnham’s first budget: will it help with the cost of living?

In his first budget as chancellor, John Healey has pledged to offer ‘breathing space’ to help Britons navigate ‘global economic storms’. There were a record number of measures, including a one-off £100 energy payment to millions and a rise in the levy on bank profits. But the Conservatives have criticised the government for postponing big decisions, including on defence and welfare. Lucy Hough speaks to economics editor Heather Stewart.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Bibi Rajinder Kaur, a 77-year-old Sikh woman, persuaded her grandson to donate some of his farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because Muslims were the only faith in her Punjab village that did not have a place to gather.Kaur isn’t alone in her generosity. Over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have worked to help restore the hundreds of mosques that were destroyed during the sectarian violence of British India’s partition in 1947. The effort has brought Muslims, Sikhs and Hindus together in this part of northern India.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says.

articles.title: Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty alleges
articles.summary: Survivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatings
body: Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report by Amnesty International.
Related: They escaped south-east Asia’s scam compounds. Then they realised they were still trapped
The global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.

“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.

Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.

“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.

“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”

Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have been lured by the promise of an office job and then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.
Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.

The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.

Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces. It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.
The rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.

“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.
Related: Trafficked, beaten and raped: raids reveal scale of abuse of women in Asia’s cyberscam centres
Scam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.
Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.

With annual losses estimated at about $100bn – a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. There are signs that some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.

In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.

“Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”
Related: Fake rooms, props and a script to lure victims: inside an abandoned Cambodia scam centre

Amnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.

Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.
Amnesty said it did not receive a response from Leap Somnang.
The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.

articles.title: Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game
articles.summary: Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street
body: Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game.

The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.
One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.

A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.

“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.
Related: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon

They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.

Activision, the game’s publisher, said that “in developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect. The game’s opening cinematic utilizes some real world news coverage to establish the game’s fictional narrative.”
“It is not intended to reference or trivialize the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form.”
The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday.
Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush.
The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.
Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.

The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.
It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.

articles.title: ‘Feels like we’ve gone backwards’: Indonesia’s choking haze provides spark for wider protests
articles.summary: After two years, President Prabowo Subianto is struggling with economic malaise, policy blunders and a devastating fire season in the world’s third-largest democracy
body: As almost 2m hectares has gone up in smoke in Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, enveloping the region in a thick dystopian haze, 33-year-old university researcher Nurul Amalia has grown increasingly exasperated.
“The government claims to be continuously increasing the number of personnel to extinguish it. But we have yet to see any significant progress,” she says.
“People in Kalimantan continue to report toxic air conditions, and now we hear news of firefighters losing their lives,” she adds, of four volunteers killed fighting fires this month.

On Wednesday, Amalia joined hundreds in Jakarta protesting against the government, the second demonstration in a week. Chief among their demands was that President Prabowo Subianto declare the fires a national disaster.

The demand is just one on a list of grievances amid brewing anger in the world’s third-largest democracy, where analysts say a confluence of policy blunders, economic stress and a government seen as increasingly out of touch is sending Indonesia into a period of volatility unseen for decades.

Civil society groups have criticised the Prabowo presidency for wasteful government programs, increasing militarisation and centralisation of power, deepening patronage, attacks on the press, and what they say is a weakened judiciary.

The government communications agency said in a statement on Wednesday that it welcomed the aspirations of student protesters as part of an effort to nurture democracy, and that concerns raised about the environment, economy and legal reform were being addressed.
Some 70,000 firefighting personnel, it added, had been sent to fire-hit regions, and it was investigating corporations and individuals allegedly involved in starting the fires.
Prabowo marked two years in power this month, but some who voted for him say the country is, at best, stagnating.
“Not only has there been no progress,” says Ika Anastasia, a PR professional and Jakartan mother of three, “it actually feels like we’ve gone backwards.
“In my 32 years, I think this government is probably the worst,” says Aryana, a private-sector employee. “The problems keep coming one after another, and before one is solved, another appears.”

Prabowo, a former military general and the ex-son-in-law of former dictator Suharto, ran in 2024 on a platform of continuity, cuddly vibes and a multibillion-dollar free meals program intended to target malnutrition.
Yet the flagship policy has been riddled with controversy.

In June this year the head of the national nutrition agency responsible for rolling out the program was arrested on allegations of corruption. Since it began, thousands of schoolchildren have been inadvertently poisoned after eating tainted meals. Among their complaints have been maggots and glass in their rice.

“This current government is strong at agenda setting in public policy, but it is very weak at delivery,” says Yanuar Nugroho, a former presidential staffer for Prabowo’s predecessor and a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS Yusof Ishak Institute.
Related: In Prabowo’s Indonesia, the military is quietly creeping back into civilian life
“Never have I seen the situation like this,” he adds. “I think this is the worst and the most messy.”

In a statement on Wednesday, the government said it would strengthen supervision and involve local government in implementing the free meals program, with many children, pregnant women and lactating mothers benefiting from it.
But a poll this month by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting showed that about 62% of Indonesians now oppose it.
The same poll gave Prabowo an approval rating of 44.5%, the lowest of any Indonesian president since polling started 20 years ago.
“It’s just a horrific result. It shows that Prabowo has lost the country,” says Kevin O’Rourke, a longtime Indonesia analyst.

“I think that it’s the programs that he’s put out are failing, and those are things that people see in their communities,” he says, referring to the free meals and a costly village cooperatives program.
Economically, Indonesia is looking a bit wobbly too.

This year the Indonesian rupiah sank to record lows against the US dollar, while the country is up to its third finance minister in two years. In recent weeks footage has shown people forming snaking lines for fuel in Bali, Sulawesi and Kalimantan.

And, in what could be a major setback for south-east Asia’s biggest economy, this month global index provider MSCI threatened to downgrade Indonesia to “standalone market” status over unclear share ownership and suspected coordinated trading.

The government pointed out the economy had grown 5.29% in the second quarter of this year and poverty had fallen by 8%, while it had accelerated market reforms to address the issues raised by the MSCI.
Some analysts say the MSCI, which is not a regulator, may have gone too far.
The president was pugilistic in his response.

“Our country continues to face all sorts of disturbances, including the MSCI. They are trying to intimidate us,” he told his cabinet. “I simply want to tell MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will never back down.”

Amid the turbulence, analysts say Prabowo has developed a reputation for being stubborn, and reluctant to accept advice. The government disputed this claim, saying Prabowo holds continuous dialogue with various stakeholders.
“I can sense on the one hand, he is detached from the reality,” observes Yanuar Nugroho. “On the other hand, he has very, very strong ideas of him as like a saviour.”
So far demonstrations have been small, but the complaints are adding up.

“There is a lot of uncertainty at the moment and we’ve seen there is a lot of potential for demonstration,” says Kennedy Muslim, an analyst from Indonesian pollster Indikator. “What it needs is a trigger, but that couldn’t be predicted.”

Indonesia is now in a situation unprecedented since its reform era began after Suharto stepped down in 1998, says O’Rourke, noting that in previous administrations there were flaws but more democratic openness, independent institutions and checks and balances.
“In the past, actors always had to respect democracy and the rules of the elections and the rights of opponents in parliament. None of that exists now,” he says.
“Prabowo has a free hand. And so it’s very ugly and very unpredictable, volatile.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce holding and demining under way to enable humanitarian corridor, Kyiv says
articles.summary: No reported incidents in 30 hours in occupied Ukrainian city. What we know on day 1,709
body: A local ceasefire in southern Ukraine was holding for a second day, both sides said on Wednesday, as hopes grew that vital aid would be able to reach stranded residents. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region amid food and medical shortages and reports many people are now starving and eating weeds. The human rights ombudsmen of both Russia and Ukraine said on Wednesday the US-brokered truce – which came into effect early on Tuesday morning – was still holding. “30 hours of the ceasefire in Oleshky have passed without a single incident,” Ukraine’s Dmytro Lubinets said. “No incidents have been recorded in the 30 hours of the ceasefire in Oleshky,” Russia’s Yana Lantratova said in a similarly worded statement. The ceasefire would be guaranteed by “the physical presence of both ombudsmen: Ukrainian and Russian” on the ground, Lubinets’s office said. Route demining was “currently under way”, Lubinets said on social media, describing it as “crucial step toward ensuring the safe delivery of humanitarian aid and enabling civilians who wish to leave the city”.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that since the ceasefire came into force, there had been “no massive attacks” on the regional capital of Kherson, where about 280,000 people lived before Russia’s invasion. “We’re happy even when we have two, three days for these people. You know, some ceasefire is great, you can see them in the streets,” the Ukrainian president told reporters in The Hague. The truce would be a “huge success” if the evacuation of Oleshky’s citizens went ahead as planned, he said.

The timing of the next round of three-way ⁠talks on a settlement of the Ukraine conflict is linked to the conflict in the Middle East, a Kremlin foreign policy aide has said, casting doubt on whether the talks will take place next month as initially proposed. Yuri Ushakov, quoted by Russian news ⁠agencies, said Moscow had not yet proposed a specific date for the talks. “It will ​also depend on the situation ‌on the battlefield and the ‌situation in general. You can see the situation now in the Middle East. It ‌just doesn’t allow us to hold it in the near future. That’s my assumption,” he told journalists on Wednesday. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he hoped a meeting would take place in Abu Dhabi between 6 and 10 November.

Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s “genius” and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine, reports Dan Sabbagh. The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation. “Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Tass news agency quoted the Russian leader as saying.

The Netherlands will supply Ukraine with €500m ($557m/£418m) ⁠in military support ⁠this ​winter, the Dutch prime minister said. The support ⁠would be used to supply drones and other material to ⁠strengthen Ukraine’s defence, Rob Jetten said ​after meeting Zelenskyy in The Hague. Earlier on ‌Wednesday, the Dutch government announced it would give Kyiv €1.2bn in non-military support in the next three years. Part of the money would be used for funds that supported ⁠Dutch companies willing to invest in the ​rebuilding ​of Ukraine.

Russian authorities have issued permits for ⁠vessels carrying grain for export to leave the Sea of Azov for the first time since 10 July, ⁠when they closed maritime ⁠traffic ​in the area due to Ukrainian drone attacks, Reuters quoted seven industry sources as saying. They said permits to pass ⁠through the Kerch Strait, which links the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, would be issued for the period ⁠to 15 November.

articles.title: Albania imposes $6,000 fine for demonstrators present at a protest that turns violent
articles.summary: The fine – six times the average monthly salary – will apply to people present at violent protests, even if they don’t personally commit violent acts
body: Albania has introduced fines of more than $6,000 for demonstrators who participate in a protest that turns violent, even if they don’t personally commit violent acts, as the government tries to clamp down on the gatherings calling for the prime minister’s resignation.
The capital, Tirana, has been racked by months of anti-government protests that in recent days have deteriorated into pitched battles between the security forces and protesters.
The leaderless movement started peacefully in May, with rallies against a luxury hotel project in a nature reserve, backed by US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Related: The Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions | Editorial

It morphed in mid-October into a wave of student-led protests against perceived corruption, shortcomings in the health system and the lack of prospects for young people in the country of 2.3 million people.

On Wednesday, prime minister Edi Rama’s government adopted legislative measures imposing fines of up to 500,000 leks (€5,500, US$6,130) for “anyone who chooses to remain in a crowd” that is carrying out acts of violence or looting in a public space, or “concealing their identity”.
The average salary before tax in Albania is €930 (US$1,026) per month.

Police were also given powers to temporarily restrict gatherings in certain areas, including near educational, healthcare and government institutions if there was a risk of violence. The measures also provide for sanctions against online incitement to violence and compensation for small businesses damaged during protests.
The measures take immediate effect but must be approved by parliament within 45 days to remain in force.

Rama said on Sunday that he was inspired by a French bill, passed by the parliament’s upper house on Wednesday, that would make protesters financially liable for damage caused during street demonstrations.
The prime minister has repeatedly blamed “foreign actors” for the violence and accused both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation. Rama has also called for “dialogue”.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself the ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to Miami
articles.summary: Far-right senator and family land in US after crossing from Brazil into Argentina and then flying via Ecuador
body: Flávio Bolsonaro declared himself the “true president” of Brazil after losing last Sunday’s presidential election and fleeing to the United States.

After landing on a private jet with his family in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday morning, the far-right senator published the claim in a letter – even though his own party has recognised the legitimate victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, as have all of Brazil’s institutions, and international observers who monitored and endorsed the vote.
Brazil’s three main newspapers – Folha de S Paulo, O Globo and O Estado de S Paulo – all described Bolsonaro’s declaration as “coup-mongering”.
The senator later deleted the letter and published a new one in which, instead of calling himself the “true president”, he described himself as “the leader of Brazil”.
Related: Lula supporters celebrate shock election victory – in pictures
After losing Sunday’s runoff vote to Lula, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.

From there he boarded a Gulfstream IV, registered LV-JQW, which had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.

Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, took off on the jet with his wife and two teenage daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil in Ecuador, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador and continued on to the Miami-Opa Locka airport, a private aviation hub about 11 miles north of downtown Miami catering to corporate executives and wealthy travelers.

Bolsonaro, wearing a black bulletproof vest and looking somber, and his family emerged from the plane into a postcard-perfect sunny south Florida morning at 9.24am. They briefly remained inside the airport before leaving, shielded by black umbrellas, climbing into a dark gray Ford Expedition Max and speeding away under police escort.

Bolsonaro said nothing to reporters before boarding the vehicle and the mood was low-key, without any supporters present to welcome him and only two dozen journalists who were kept at a distance by two Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents.

In the letter, published about seven hours after his arrival, Bolsonaro also thanked Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, “for his courage, sense of justice and legality”, and Donald Trump “and the wonderful American people for welcoming me”.

He again repeated, without evidence, his claim that there had been “electoral fraud” – a claim rejected by Brazil’s electoral court and supreme court, as well as the presidents of the lower house and senate. Bolsonaro’s party said on Monday: “We recognise the presidential result.”

At least three different versions of the letter were published by Bolsonaro and his allies, including one that used the country’s pre-1968 name and the English spelling “Brazil” rather than the Portuguese “Brasil” – which some saw as another sign of the Bolsonaro clan’s subservience to the US.
Brazilian newspapers reported that Bolsonaro and his family had been granted humanitarian visas in the US. On Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.
“They’re fine people. … I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flávio a little bit. I know the father very well,” the US president said.
On Wednesday, however, when asked about Bolsonaro’s claim, Trump said he would stay out of Brazil’s post-election turmoil.

“Well, I’m not going to make a comment about that, but I know that we gave him a pass to come into the country, so we’ll see,” he said. “But I won’t get involved. It was a very strange election, that’s for sure.”

Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.

Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan to go through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him from leaving the country.

There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies, at about 6pm on Monday, and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.
Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.

The Argentinian newspaper Página/12 reported that the aircraft belonged to the businessman Sergio Daniel Mastropietro, who was investigated by local police in one of the biggest scandals of Javier Milei’s administration, involving the alleged payment of bribes linked to the purchase of medicines for people with disabilities.

Bolsonaro is under investigation in at least two criminal cases, one of them examining suspicions that the senator was involved in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.

It was in connection with that case that, shortly after the election result, Brazilian police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.

Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.

O Globo newspaper reported that the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.

Fleeing Brazil has almost become standard practice among Bolsonaro supporters facing criminal charges or convictions in the country: about a dozen politicians or influencers closely aligned with Jair Bolsonaro have done the same in recent years.

The former president himself spent three months in Florida shortly after losing the 2022 election. He later returned to Brazil and, while facing trial over the attempted coup, spent two nights at the Hungarian embassy in Brasília, then run by his ally Viktor Orbán.
While under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison, the patriarch of the Bolsonaro clan used a soldering iron in an attempt to destroy his electronic ankle monitor.

articles.title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks
articles.summary: Watered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’
body: The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between member states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.

A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.

The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.
The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.
It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.

But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.
Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.

Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.

At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.
Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.

Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.

Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.

A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.
Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.

Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.

articles.title: US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way
articles.summary: Pete Hoekstra, controversial US ambassador to Canada, has also accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections
body: The US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries.

On Wednesday, CTV news reported that Pete Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it.
“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations.
For months, Canada and the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada.
Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.

Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”.

This year a House of Commons petition signed by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country.

More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television.

“We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it. And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recently told a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”.

Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”.
Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.

Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.
“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said.

“His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. I don’t think that he’s serving American interests very well. I’m not even sure that he’s serving the interests of his president.”

Paris points to polling in the US that shows voters have increasingly linked tariffs, the war and cost of living. There is also widespread confusion over why the White House has chosen to treat Canada as a trade adversary.

“It’s certainly not working in Canada. It’s on the contrary. It seems that every time Mr Hoekstra opens his mouth, the Canadians are more determined than before to stand up to the bullying of the Trump administration,” he said. “That’s not serving American interests.”
The US embassy denied Hoekstra said Canada would face blame for a poor Republican showing, suggesting the remarks were “grossly taken out of context” from a broader discussion.

“The ambassador has consistently said that the Canadian media is attempting to overstate the relevance of Canadian issues in American elections. As we have previously stated, Americans will decide American elections based on issues that are important to them,” the embassy said in a statement.

At a Canadian American Business event last year, Hoekstra delivered what witnesses say was an expletive-laden tirade at Ontario’s trade representative after the province ran a series of anti-tariff ads in the US that featured Ronald Reagan. Ontario’s premier called the outburst “absolutely unacceptable” and “unbecoming of an ambassador”.

Last week, Barack Obama noted the unusual choice to attack a longtime ally while speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit, mocking Trump’s fixation on Canada and jokingly referring to his northern neighbor as a “well-known evil empire”.

“That historical adversary of ours: Canada,” the former US president said. “It’s your neighbor! It’s a few minutes drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup. They are the nicest people. And somehow we’ve gotten them so mad.”

articles.title: Coalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majority
articles.summary: Projections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that drew highest turnout in decades
body: Israel’s future hung in the balance on Wednesday as it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu had lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.

The leader of the Jewish opposition bloc, the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, appeared to rule out such a broad coalition in a premature declaration of victory overnight for what he called a “Zionist majority”.

As the vote count proceeded on Wednesday, initial exit poll projections that Eisenkot’s bloc would have a narrow lead over Netanyahu’s coalition looked increasingly in doubt as the prime minister’s bloc edged ahead, with the votes of deployed soldiers and other absentee ballots – about 14% of the total electorate – yet to be fully counted.

With the remaining 86% of the votes tallied, both Jewish blocs looked certain to fall short of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority government, leaving Eisenkot and his allies facing a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 16-19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

On Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and the success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming they had “stolen the election”. He did not offer evidence, but said on X that his Likud party had sent “hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence” to the central elections committee and the Shin Bet internal security agency.

Both those agencies have been politicised under Netanyahu’s government. The elections committee had sought to ban Arab Israeli parties before the poll, but the attempt to exclude them was overturned by the country’s supreme court.

Donald Trump took credit for Netanyahu’s better than expected performance so far, claiming his overt backing in the run-up to the vote had made the difference. “When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said, adding that the result appeared to be heading for a stalemate or a Netanyahu win.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s Change bloc, urged Eisenkot to negotiate with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am (the United Arab List).
“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid. And if we don’t put an end to racism. We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” Golan wrote on X.
Related: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

“Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel,” he added, pointing out that Netanyahu relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that were non-Zionist and opposed conscription for their constituents.

Noa Landau, a commenter writing in Haaretz, argued that by making Zionism the test for forming a coalition, excluding potential partners, while the prime minister had not, Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.

The Joint List leader, Yousef Jabareen, said its strong performance meant it “can’t be ignored under any political scenario”. He said Netanyahu’s government, especially its extremist national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, “has made life bitter for every Arab citizen”.

“We will be ready to pave the way to oust the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – and send them home,” Jabareen said. Another Joint List official described the choice facing the Jewish opposition as “supremacy or building democracy”.

Counting all the votes could take another few days, with absentee ballots the last to be tallied. Most of those are from deployed soldiers. The army vote usually swings right, but that broad picture may be complicated by the fact that a lot of older, more moderate reservists are now on active duty.

Once all the votes are accounted for, it will be up to Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, to give one of the party leaders six weeks to form a government. If the first choice fails, the opportunity passes to their rival. In the weeks of political wrangling likely to ensue, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are expected to lure defectors from each other’s camps.

Netanyahu would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new majority is formed. He might expect to benefit if the deadlock leads to another round of elections. Tens of thousands of diaspora Israelis who returned to vote on Tuesday, and were mostly opposed to the governing coalition, might not return for another vote, for example.

The Palestinian parties and Jewish centre-left have been urging the opposition to focus on finding common cause in the Knesset, replacing the speaker and pursuing legislation that the factions can agree on, such as ordering an independent review into the security failures that led to the 7 October attack by Hamas in 2023.
On Wednesday, Herzog urged all parties to keep an “open mind” in trying to build a new government coalition.
“We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said.

The election happened in the midst of Israel’s war in Gaza – barely mentioned in the course of the campaign, despite the fact that Israel has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and Netanyahu is wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes.

A UN commission of human rights experts reported on Monday that Israel had continued to commit genocidal acts against Palestinian civilians in Gaza after a ceasefire was declared in October 2025. Since then 1,431 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military, including 300 children.

The report, by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said: “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”

Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Daniel Meron, rejected the report as an “attempt to destroy the Jewish state” and “to undermine Israel’s ​legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself”.

Eisenkot and much of his bloc support the war in Gaza, and sought to make the election a referendum on Netanyahu. The turnout was nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting.
Political deadlock has led to repeated votes in the past. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.

Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, governing for 19 of the past 30 years, and its most tenacious political survivor. Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, he and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.
The campaign, febrile even by Israeli standards, included Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.

Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023, Israel has devastated Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war alongside the US against Iran.
